A **freelancer** is a self-employed person who sells a service to several clients, one project or one month at a time. There is no employer paying a salary, no fixed office and no one handing out work. You are a one-person business: you find the client, agree the job, do it, send the bill and make sure you are paid. That is why this course treats freelancing as a business skill, not only a talent.

Freelancing is different from selling products. A trader buys stock and sells it again. A freelancer sells **time, skill and results**: a written article, a cleaned-up spreadsheet, a month of social media posts, a translated document, a set of bookkeeping records. You cannot store a service on a shelf, so every naira you earn is tied to work you actually deliver.

The freelance client cycle

Every freelance job, small or large, passes through the same six stages. Beginners often focus only on stage four, doing the work, and are surprised when the money does not come. Each stage needs its own skill, and this course has a lesson for each one.
Find the client
Pitch and discuss
Agree scope and price
Deliver the work
Invoice and get paid
Keep and get referrals
Each finished job feeds the next one through repeat work and referrals, so the cycle gets easier the longer you keep it turning.
**Find:** let the right people know your service exists (your network, platforms, direct messages).
**Pitch:** reply to a need with a short, specific message and a sample.
**Agree:** put the scope, deadline, price and payment terms in writing before you start.
**Deliver:** do the work to the agreed standard, on time, with clear updates.
**Get paid:** send a proper invoice and collect a deposit or full payment.
**Keep:** ask for feedback and a testimonial, and offer the next piece of work.
Billable and non-billable hours

A **billable hour** is an hour you spend doing work a client pays for. A **non-billable hour** is business work nobody pays you for directly: looking for clients, writing pitches, answering enquiries that go nowhere, sending invoices, learning, and fixing your own laptop. Many experienced freelancers find that a large share of their week, often a quarter to a half, is non-billable, especially in the first year. If you price your work as though every hour is paid, you will earn far less than you planned.
Worked example: how many hours can actually earn money?
For example, Amaka in Ibadan has two school-age children. She can work from 9 am to 2 pm on weekdays and for two hours on Saturday.
Weekday hours: 5 hours x 5 days = 25 hours. Saturday adds 2 hours, so 27 working hours a week.
She sets aside 1 hour a day on weekdays for finding clients and admin: 5 hours a week.
She allows another 4 hours a week for unpaid revisions, calls and learning.
Billable hours left: 27 minus 5 minus 4 = 18 hours a week.
Over a month of about 4 weeks: 18 x 4 = 72 billable hours, not 108.
Amaka will plan her income around 72 paid hours a month. In Module 2 she will use this number to work out her minimum rate, instead of guessing.
Freelancing is not passive income

Your income stops when you stop working, and there is no paid leave or pension unless you create it yourself. The upside is control: you choose your clients, your hours and your prices, and you can raise them as your skill and reputation grow.
Is this the right time for you?

Freelancing suits women who need flexible hours, have a skill other people struggle with, and can tolerate months when income is uneven. It is harder if you need a fixed amount every month starting next week, because most new freelancers take weeks or months to land steady clients. Many women start freelancing alongside a job, trade or studies, then grow it gradually. That is a sensible path, not a weakness.

The most common beginner mistake is offering everything: "I do writing, design, typing, social media, anything you need." It feels safer, but clients hire people who look like a clear answer to one problem. A business owner with a messy Instagram page wants a social media manager, not someone who might be able to help with it among ten other things. Your first job in freelancing is to choose **one service** and make it easy to understand.
Step 1: list what you can already do

Start with skills you have used for real, at work, in church or community groups, in school or for family. Write each as a task, not a quality. "Organised" is a quality. "Keeps a monthly expense spreadsheet for our cooperative" is a task someone could pay for.
Step 2: test demand with evidence
Demand means people are already paying, or actively asking, for this service. You can find evidence in about an hour with your phone:
**Job and gig sites:** search the service on Upwork, Fiverr, LinkedIn Jobs or Jobberman and note how many recent posts or sellers you see.
**Local businesses:** look at five businesses near you or on Instagram. Is their menu badly designed, their page silent for months, their price list unclear?
**Your network:** ask ten people who run businesses: "Do you pay anyone for this, or wish you could?"
**WhatsApp and Facebook groups:** search business groups you already belong to for requests like "I need someone to..."
Many sellers is a good sign
If you find many freelancers already offering a service, that usually proves people buy it. It means you must be more specific, not that you should give up. No sellers at all can mean no buyers.

Worked example: choosing between three skills
For example, Hauwa in Kaduna can type fast, designs flyers for her church in Canva, and speaks Hausa and English fluently.

Step 4: write your offer line

An **offer line** is one sentence that tells a stranger exactly what you do. Use this pattern: **I help [specific client] get [result they want] by [your service].** It names who it is for, why they would care, and what you actually do.
Too broad
Specific offer line

Notice that the specific lines also hint at the deliverable (product descriptions, 12 posts a month), which makes pricing easier later. Avoid promising results you cannot control, such as "double your sales". You can promise the work and a reasonable benefit, not the client's profit.

Choosing one service now does not lock you in forever. Freelancers often start narrow, build a reputation, and then add related services that the same clients ask for. Narrow first makes the first clients come faster.

Before you look for clients, make sure you can actually do the work, get paid and stay safe. A client who waits two days because your data ran out, or a payment that never arrives because you used an unsafe channel, can undo weeks of effort. This lesson is your readiness checklist.
Tools and connection

Much freelance work can start on a smartphone: writing in Google Docs, designing in Canva, managing WhatsApp Business, keeping records in Google Sheets. Some services, such as long documents, spreadsheets or design files for print, are much easier on a laptop. Be honest about what your service needs. You also need a reliable connection: keep a backup, such as a second SIM on a different network, and know where you can go if power or data fails on a deadline day.
**A professional email address:** firstname.lastname or a business name on Gmail, not a nickname.
**Cloud storage:** Google Drive or similar, so work is not lost if your phone is stolen or damaged.
**A calendar:** Google Calendar for deadlines and client calls, with reminders switched on.
**WhatsApp Business:** a separate business profile with your offer line and working hours.
**Two-step verification** switched on for email and WhatsApp, so a stolen password is not enough to take over your accounts.

Your money buffer

New freelancers usually have uneven months. A **buffer** is savings that cover your essential costs while you build clients, so you are not forced to accept bad jobs out of panic. A common rule of thumb is to aim for about three months of essential costs. If you cannot save that yet, keep your current income source while you start, and grow the buffer from your first freelance earnings.
Worked example: working out a buffer
For example, Chioma in Lagos plans to freelance as a virtual assistant while keeping her part-time shop job for now. All figures are approximate.
Her essential monthly costs: rent share 60,000 naira, food 70,000, transport 25,000, data and airtime 15,000, children's school costs averaged per month 30,000. Total: 200,000 naira.
Three months of essentials: 200,000 x 3 = 600,000 naira.
Her shop job pays enough to cover 150,000 a month, leaving a gap of 50,000 a month.
Buffer for her actual gap over three months: 50,000 x 3 = 150,000 naira.
She plans to save 25 percent of every freelance payment until the 150,000 buffer is complete.
Because she keeps her job, Chioma needs a 150,000 naira buffer, not 600,000. She will consider leaving the job only when freelance income has covered the gap for several months in a row.
Scams that target freelancers
Wherever people look for work online, scammers follow. Learn the patterns so you can say no quickly.
Red flags: stop and check
Asks you to pay first
Overpays, then wants refund
Moves chat off platform fast
Huge pay for little work
Asks for codes or passwords
Unpaid big test task
If any of these appear, pause, verify the client independently, and do not send money or codes.
**Pay to work:** a "client" asks you to pay for training, software or a registration fee before you can start. Real clients pay you, not the other way round.
**Overpayment refund:** someone sends more than agreed, by cheque or a transfer that later reverses, then begs you to refund the extra. The original payment disappears and your refund is gone.
**Account takeover:** someone asks for the six-digit code sent to your phone. That code lets them take over your WhatsApp or bank account. Never share it.
**Free work disguised as a test:** a short sample is normal. Writing ten full articles or designing a full brand "as a test" is unpaid work.
Protect client data too

Clients may share customer lists, passwords or private documents. Keep them only as long as needed, do not forward them, and use the client's own shared folders where possible. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data, and careful handling also protects your reputation.

Clients rarely want to buy "hours". They want a finished result: 20 product descriptions, a month of posts, a translated survey. A **package** is a fixed bundle of work with a clear price, so the client knows exactly what they get and you know exactly what to do. Behind every package price, though, you need a number only you see: your **minimum hourly rate**, the lowest amount per working hour that keeps your business alive.
Your minimum rate in three steps
From income target to package price
Monthly income target
Add business costs
Divide by billable hours
Minimum hourly rate
Hours per job x rate
Your package price starts from what you need to earn, not from the cheapest price you have seen online.
Decide your monthly **income target**: what you want to take home from freelancing each month.
Add your monthly **business costs**: data, electricity or fuel for power, software subscriptions, saving towards a new laptop or phone, and money you set aside for tax.
Divide the total by your **billable hours** per month, from Module 1. The answer is your minimum hourly rate.
Worked example: Amaka's minimum rate and package price
For example, Amaka writes product descriptions for small online shops. She has 72 billable hours a month (from Module 1). All naira figures are approximate.
Income target: 250,000 naira a month.
Business costs: data 15,000, power and fuel 15,000, saving for a laptop 10,000. Total costs: 40,000 naira.
Total needed: 250,000 + 40,000 = 290,000 naira.
Minimum hourly rate: 290,000 / 72 = about 4,028 naira. She rounds up to 4,100 naira an hour.
She times herself: 20 product descriptions take about 6 hours to write plus 2 hours for checks and one revision round, so 8 hours.
Package cost to her: 8 x 4,100 = 32,800 naira. She prices the package at 35,000 naira.
Amaka now knows that any offer below about 33,000 naira for 20 descriptions loses her money in time. She can still choose to discount for a portfolio client, but she will do it knowingly.
Time yourself honestly
Do one practice job and record every minute: reading the brief, research, the work itself, checking, and messaging. Beginners nearly always underestimate the time, especially the messaging.

Each package should also say what is outside it, for example "product photography not included" or "posting to the shop website is extra". This protects you later when a client asks for "one small thing" that is really a new job. You will use this in the written agreement two lessons from now.
Fees and international clients

If you work through a freelance platform, it keeps a service fee from what the client pays, and moving money to your bank can cost a withdrawal or exchange fee. These change over time, so always read the platform's current fee page before you set prices. Then quote high enough that **what reaches your account** still covers your minimum rate.
Worked example: allowing for fees
For example, Hauwa is quoted on a platform that, in this illustration, keeps 10 percent of each payment. She wants at least 90 US dollars to reach her account for a translation job.
If she quotes 90 dollars, she receives 90 x 0.90 = 81 dollars. Too low.
To receive 90 dollars after a 10 percent fee, she divides: 90 / 0.90 = 100 dollars.
She also checks the withdrawal cost and exchange rate before converting to naira.
Hauwa quotes 100 dollars. She works out fees by dividing, not by adding 10 percent, because 90 + 9 = 99 would still leave her short.

Quote international clients in their own currency, usually US dollars, pounds or euros, and do not simply convert your naira price. Look at what freelancers with similar experience charge on the same platform, then check that your price still meets your minimum rate after fees.
Minimum hourly rate = (income target + business costs) / billable hours.
Package price = estimated hours x minimum rate, rounded up.

Choose **two channels** and use them steadily for a month rather than trying all of them for a week. Your warm network is usually the fastest first channel, because people already trust you.

The four-part pitch
**Notice something specific** about their business: "I saw your Instagram has great cake photos but no prices in the captions."
**Offer one clear service** linked to it, using your offer line.
**Show proof**: one link or one image of a sample, not your whole life story.
**Ask for a small next step**: "Can I send you three sample captions for free this week?" or "Would a 10-minute call on Thursday work?"
Worked example: a pitch to a bakery
For example, Ifeoma in Enugu offers Instagram caption writing and sees a home bakery whose posts have photos but no prices or ordering steps.
Message: "Good afternoon, Mrs Ada. I love the red velvet cakes on your page. I noticed most posts do not say the price or how to order, which can make customers scroll past."
"I write short Instagram captions for home bakers that include the price, size and a simple order step."
"Here is a sample I wrote for a cake shop in Nsukka: [link]."
"Would you like me to rewrite three of your recent captions so you can see the difference? No cost for those three."
The message is under 90 words, personal, and asks for a tiny yes. Three free captions take Ifeoma about 30 minutes and show her skill far better than a long CV would.
Free samples have limits

A small sample of two or three items is reasonable when you are new. Do not give away whole projects. Decide in advance the maximum time you will spend on any free sample, for example 30 to 45 minutes.
Follow up, then stop

Busy people miss messages. A polite follow-up often gets more replies than the first message. A simple rhythm: send the pitch, follow up after 3 or 4 days with one short line, and send a final note about a week later. Then stop and move on. Never send messages late at night, and respect any "no, thank you" immediately.

When a potential client replies "How much?" or "Let's talk", the job is not yet won. Many freelance disputes start right here, when both sides agree in a hurry and later remember the job differently. The discovery conversation

A **discovery call** is a short conversation, 10 to 20 minutes by phone, WhatsApp call or Google Meet, where you find out what the client really needs. You talk less and ask more. Use these questions and write the answers down:
What do you need done, and what prompted it now?
Who is it for, and what should they do or feel after seeing it?
Do you have examples you like, or materials I should use (logo, photos, old documents)?
When do you need it, and is that date fixed?
Who gives the final approval?
What budget have you set aside for this?

Deposits and payment terms

A **deposit** is part payment before you start. It shows the client is serious and protects you if they disappear. Many freelancers ask for 50 percent up front for new clients, with the balance before final files are released. For larger projects you can split payment into milestones, for example 40 percent, 30 percent and 30 percent. For international platform jobs, use the platform's own payment protection, such as funded milestones, rather than moving the payment outside the platform.
Worked example: handling an extra request

For example, Zainab in Abuja agreed to design 12 posts for 60,000 naira, about 5,000 naira per post. On day 4 the client asks her to "also make a quick flyer for the Christmas promo and 3 more posts".
She checks the scope: the flyer and 3 extra posts are not included.
She replies warmly: "Happy to help with these. They are outside our current scope, so here is a quick change request."
Extra posts: 3 x 5,000 = 15,000 naira. Flyer: her design rate for a flyer is 12,000 naira. Total change: 27,000 naira.
She adds one extra day to the deadline because of the added work and asks for the change to be paid with the final balance.
The client agrees in writing. The new total is 60,000 + 27,000 = 87,000 naira, and the extra work is paid instead of quietly absorbed.
When the client hesitates

Some clients agree on the call, then go quiet when the deposit is mentioned. Send one friendly reminder after two or three days: "Just checking whether you would like to go ahead with the December posts. I am holding a slot for you until Friday." If they say the price is too high, offer a smaller package instead of cutting the price of the same work. For example, offer 8 posts instead of 12 rather than 12 posts for less money. If there is still no answer after your reminder, release the slot and move on without bitterness. Many quiet clients come back months later.
Scope creep

**Scope creep** is when a job slowly grows through many "small" extra requests. It is the main reason freelancers end up working for very little per hour. Answer every extra request kindly, then price it.

Clients come back to freelancers who are **reliable**, not only talented. In practice, reliable means three things: you deliver what was agreed, you deliver when you said, and the client never has to chase you for news. This lesson gives you a simple workflow that makes all three normal.

Five-stage delivery workflow

Following the same five stages on every job makes your quality steady, even on busy weeks.
**Kick-off:** confirm the scope, collect every material the client promised (logo, photos, documents) and say when the first draft will arrive.
**Plan backwards:** put the client deadline in your calendar, then set your own earlier deadline with a buffer for power cuts, data problems or illness.
**Draft and self-check:** do the work, then check it line by line against the written scope before the client sees it.
**Revisions:** collect all the client's changes in one message per round, make them, and confirm when a round is finished.
**Handover:** send final files with clear names, in the right format, with a short note on how to use them.
Worked example: planning backwards with a buffer
For example, Zainab agrees to deliver 12 social media designs in 7 working days. She works about 4 billable hours a day.
She estimates 12 hours of design and 3 hours for one revision round: 15 hours in total.
She adds a buffer of about 20 percent: 15 x 1.2 = 18 hours, or 4 and a half working days at 4 hours a day.
She has 7 working days, so she sets her own target to send final files on day 6, one day before the client deadline.
She schedules: drafts sent on day 3, client feedback by the end of day 4, revisions on day 5, final checks and handover on day 6.
She tells the client: "You will receive drafts on day 3. Please send all changes in one message by the evening of day 4 so I can finish on time."
Zainab delivers a day early even after a power cut on day 5 costs her 3 hours, because the buffer absorbed it.
Ask for feedback in one message
Ask clients to collect all their changes into one message per revision round. Scattered voice notes over several days are the fastest way to miss a change and blow a deadline.
The self-check before anything is sent

Put the written scope next to your work and tick each item. Then add checks for your service. A writer reads the text aloud once and runs a spelling check, then confirms every name, price and phone number against the client's materials. A designer checks the size in pixels, the spelling on every design, and that the client's logo and colours are correct. A virtual assistant checks that every calendar entry has the right date and time zone. Errors in names, prices and phone numbers are the ones clients notice first and forgive least.

Agree how and when you will communicate: WhatsApp for quick questions, email for files and approvals, and your working hours. A simple rule many freelancers use is to reply to client messages within one working day, even if the reply is only "Received, I will send the answer by 3 pm tomorrow."

If something will be late, say so **as soon as you know**, not on the deadline day. Give the reason in one line, a new date, and what the client will receive in the meantime. Clients forgive an early warning far more easily than a silent delay.

Ethical freelancing
**Capacity:** only accept work you can deliver well on time. Saying "I can start on the 15th" is better than accepting and failing.
**Honesty about skill:** do not claim experience you do not have. Say "I have done this for two clients" rather than "I am an expert".
**Confidentiality:** do not share client documents, customer lists or private messages, and do not post client work publicly without permission.
**Original work:** do not copy other people's writing or designs; use properly licensed fonts, images and music.
**AI tools:** if you use AI to draft or design, check every fact and word yourself, follow the client's rules, and be honest if they ask how the work was made.
When a client is unhappy

Sometimes a client says the work is not what they wanted. Stay calm and go back to the written scope together. If you missed something that was agreed, fix it quickly and without extra charge. If the client now wants something different from what was agreed, explain kindly that this is a change and offer a price for it. If you truly cannot satisfy a client, a partial refund of the unfinished part can be a fair way to close the job, and it protects your reputation. Never argue in public comments or reviews.
Do not move platform clients off the platform

If you met a client on a freelance platform, taking payment outside it usually breaks the platform's terms and removes its payment protection. Your account can be closed and you lose the protection if the client does not pay.

For self-employed people, personal income tax is handled by the internal revenue service of the state where you live, and you may need a Tax Identification Number (TIN). Rules change, so ask your state revenue service or a qualified tax adviser what applies to you. Whatever the rules, keep every invoice, payment confirmation and business expense receipt in one folder by month. Good records make tax, loans and planning much easier.

Some freelancers move a fixed share of every payment into a separate savings pocket for tax and business costs as soon as it arrives. The exact share is a personal decision, but the habit stops you spending money that is not really yours to spend.

Effective hourly rate

Your **effective hourly rate** is what you really earned for every hour you worked on your freelance business: money received divided by all working hours, billable and non-billable. Compare it with the minimum rate you calculated in Module 2.
Worked example: a busy month that paid too little
For example, Amaka's minimum rate is 4,100 naira an hour. In March she received payment for five jobs.
Billable hours on those jobs: 60. Rate on billable hours: 180,000 / 60 = 3,000 naira.
Non-billable hours (outreach, calls, admin): 30. Total hours: 90.
Effective hourly rate: 180,000 / 90 = 2,000 naira, less than half her minimum rate.
Looking at her tracker, two jobs ran over their estimated hours because of unplanned revision rounds, and she spent 12 hours on free samples.
Amaka decides on two changes for April: a firm limit of 2 revision rounds stated in every scope, and a maximum of 30 minutes per free sample.
Three more useful numbers

**Average job value:** total money received divided by number of jobs. 180,000 / 5 = 36,000 naira. Raising this, for example by selling the Standard package more often, is often easier than finding more clients.
**Repeat client rate:** clients who came back divided by total clients. If 2 of 5 clients in a quarter were returning clients, that is 2 / 5 = 40 percent. Repeat clients cost far less time to win.
**Outreach conversion:** paying clients divided by messages sent, from your funnel in Module 2.
Look at trends, not one month
Freelance income goes up and down. Compare each number with the previous two or three months before drawing conclusions. One slow month does not mean you have failed.
Turning numbers into targets

Your numbers also tell you how much work you need. Divide your monthly money target by your average job value to see how many jobs you need. Then use your outreach conversion to see how many messages that takes. If the answer is unrealistic, the fix is usually to raise the value of each job or win more repeat work, not to send hundreds more messages.

For example, Amaka needs 290,000 naira a month (her income target plus business costs from Module 2). Her average job value is 36,000 naira and 1 in 40 outreach messages becomes a client.

If every job came from cold outreach: 9 x 40 = 360 messages a month, which is not realistic alongside the work itself.
If 4 of the 9 jobs are repeat clients, she needs only 5 new clients: 5 x 40 = 200 messages. Still heavy.
If she also lifts her average job value to 50,000 naira by promoting Premium and monthly packages: 290,000 / 50,000 = 5.8, so 6 jobs.
With 3 of those 6 from repeat clients, she needs 3 new clients: 3 x 40 = 120 messages a month, about 6 a working day.
Amaka sees that repeat work and bigger packages, not more messages alone, make her target reachable. These become the focus of Module 4.

People will ask "So what do you do?" at weddings, in church, in the market and on calls. Prepare a short answer in three parts and practise it aloud until it feels natural.
**Who and what:** your offer line. "I help home bakers get more orders by writing Instagram captions that include price and how to order."
**Proof:** one result. "One bakery in Enugu told me customers now ask fewer questions before ordering."
**Invitation:** a light next step. "If you know a baker who struggles with posting, I would love to help."
Two people shaking hands over a deal
A clear explanation of value turns a casual chat into a client conversation.
Use the client's own numbers

The most convincing value statements use numbers the client already knows. Ask on the discovery call: "How many hours a week do you spend on this now?" or "How many customers ask the same question before ordering?" If a coach says she spends 6 hours a week on email and booking, and your service gives most of those hours back, she can judge for herself what that time is worth to her. You do not need to promise sales figures. You help the client see the cost of the problem they already have.

With international clients on platforms, the same idea applies in writing. Open your proposal with their problem in your own words, state the outcome you will deliver, and list exactly what is included. Clients reading many proposals quickly notice the one that shows it understood the job.
When a client says "too expensive"
Treat "too expensive" as a question, not a final no. Stay calm and find out what they are comparing you to. Then choose one of these responses:
**Reduce the scope, not the rate:** "For 35,000 naira I can do 20 descriptions. Within 18,000 I can do the 10 most important products first."
**Split the payment:** offer staged payments, for example half now and half on delivery, if cash flow is the real problem.
**Explain what is included:** revisions, research, quick turnaround, and your record of results.
**Let it go politely:** if the budget is far below your minimum rate, thank them and leave the door open. Not every client is your client.
Why not just give a discount?

Cutting the price for the same work teaches the client that your first price was not real, and it pushes you below your minimum rate. If you do discount, attach it to something real: a longer commitment, payment in full up front, or permission to use the job as a portfolio case.
Monthly packages

A **retainer** or monthly package is an agreement for the same service every month, for example 12 social posts or 10 hours of virtual assistance. It gives the client steady support and gives you predictable income with less selling. Agree the monthly scope, the payment date (usually at the start of the month), what happens to unused hours, and how either side can end it, for example with 30 days' notice.
Worked example: offering a monthly package
For example, Zainab's client paid 60,000 naira for 12 one-off posts that took her 15 hours. The client now asks for posts every month.
One-off rate earned: 60,000 / 15 = 4,000 naira an hour.
Because she now knows the brand, she estimates each month will take 11 hours.
She offers a 3-month package at 55,000 naira a month, paid on the 1st, with 30 days' notice to end.
Her rate on the package: 55,000 / 11 = 5,000 naira an hour, higher than before even with the lower price.
Three months of income secured: 55,000 x 3 = 165,000 naira without new outreach.
The client pays less per month, and Zainab earns more per hour with steady income. Both sides gain because repeat work takes less time.
Raising your rates

As your skill, speed and proof grow, your prices should grow too. Raise prices for **new** clients first. For existing clients, give written notice, for example 30 days, and thank them for their support. A small, regular rise is easier for clients to accept than a big jump after years of the same price.

Building a 90-day plan

Ninety days is long enough to see real results from steady outreach and short enough to stay focused. Split it into three 30-day phases, each with one main goal, weekly activity targets, and a number to check at the end.
90 days in three phases

Days 31 to 60: proof and process
Days 61 to 90: repeat and raise
Each phase builds on the one before: clients first, then proof, then steadier and better-paid work.
Worked example: Hauwa's 90-day plan
For example, Hauwa offers Hausa to English and English to Hausa translation. She can give 15 hours a week. Her launch project produced 3 pitches, 1 reply and no paid job yet.
Days 1 to 30: send 5 personal pitches a week to NGOs, researchers and media houses (20 in total), complete her LinkedIn profile, and win 1 to 2 first clients. Check: reply rate.
Days 31 to 60: keep 5 pitches a week, deliver every job with her scope and invoice templates, and collect 2 testimonials. Check: effective hourly rate against her minimum of 4,500 naira.
Days 61 to 90: offer a monthly or multi-document package to her best client, ask two happy clients for referrals, and raise her price for new clients by 10 percent. Check: repeat client rate.
Total planned pitches: 5 a week x about 13 weeks = 65 pitches.
At her current rate of 1 reply per 3 pitches, 65 pitches should bring 65 / 3 = about 21 or 22 replies, enough conversations to test and improve her calls.
Hauwa's plan is specific, measurable and fits her 15 hours a week. Her monthly review dates are fixed in her calendar for days 30, 60 and 90.
Plan for weeks that go wrong
Illness, family events and power cuts will happen. Build in one lighter week per month and decide in advance what the minimum is for a hard week, for example 2 pitches and one tracker update.

**Targets with no activity:** "earn 300,000 naira" without saying how many pitches or packages that needs.

**No review dates:** a plan nobody checks becomes a wish.
**Ignoring time:** planning 30 hours of work a week when you have 15.

Your first clients are hard to win because strangers have no proof that you are good.
Every finished job is a chance to create that proof. Ask for feedback, collect a testimonial, and record what you achieved.
Then offer the next piece of work, because repeat clients take far less time to win.

Step by step
Collect a strong testimonial
Ask within a few days of handover
Ask specific questions
Type up her words and ask permission
Write a three-line case snapshot
Never write a testimonial yourself or invent results
Ask while the client is still pleased. For example, Ifeoma finished a month of captions for Ada's Cakes and messaged four days later.
General questions get answers like good job, thanks. So ask: what was the main problem before, what has changed since, and what could I do better?
Ada replied with a voice note. Ifeoma typed up the key sentences and asked: may I use these words, with your name and business, on my page? Ada agreed.
Then Ifeoma wrote a case snapshot in three lines. Problem: posts had no prices. Work: 12 captions with price, size and order steps. Result: customers now ask fewer questions before ordering.
Use the client's own words for the result. Never invent numbers like sales doubled, and never put a client's name on words you wrote yourself.
Keep the cycle turning
Referrals and the next job
Keep proof in one Drive folder
Show your best two or three pieces
Ask once for a referral
Offer a concrete next piece of work
Keep all your proof in one Google Drive folder, so you can send the right item in seconds.
Show your best two or three pieces where clients look: your WhatsApp Business catalogue, LinkedIn, or your platform profile.
After positive feedback, ask simply, once: if you know another business owner who could use this, please share my number.
And at every handover, suggest a next piece of work with a package name and price, so saying yes is easy.
Price conversations
When a client says too expensive
Do
Reduce the scope, not the rate
Offer staged payments
Explain what is included
Let it go politely
Avoid
Same work for less money
Going below your minimum rate
Arguing or begging
Treat too expensive as a question, not a final no. Find out what they are comparing you to.

Then reduce the scope, not the rate. For 35,000 naira I can do 20 descriptions. Within 18,000 I can do the 10 most important first. You can also split the payment, or let a very low budget go politely.

Cutting the price for the same work teaches the client your first price was not real, and pushes you below your minimum rate. If you discount, attach it to something real, like payment in full up front.
Worked example
A monthly package pays better
For example, Zainab's client paid 60,000 naira for 12 posts and now wants posts every month.
One-off job, per hour
Monthly package, per month
Monthly package, per hour
Total is three months of secured income.
A monthly package, also called a retainer, is the same service every month. It gives you predictable income with less selling.
The one-off job took Zainab 15 hours, so she earned 4,000 naira an hour.
Now she knows the brand, so she offers 3 months at 55,000 naira a month, paid on the 1st, with 30 days' notice to end.
Each month takes about 11 hours, so she now earns 5,000 naira an hour, even at a lower price.
And she has secured 165,000 naira over three months, without new outreach. Both sides gain.
Your 90-day plan
Three phases of 30 days
Review dates fixed in your calendar
For example, Hauwa can give 15 hours a week. In the first 30 days she sends 5 personal pitches a week and aims for 1 to 2 first clients.
In days 31 to 60, she keeps pitching, uses her templates on every job and collects 2 testimonials.
In days 61 to 90, she offers a monthly package, asks for referrals, and raises her price for new clients by 10 percent.
Her review dates are fixed for days 30, 60 and 90. Avoid the common mistakes: targets with no activity, too many channels, and planning more hours than you have.

Remember
Ask specific feedback questions
Testimonials need permission, never invented
Reduce scope, not your rate
Monthly packages build steady income

To remember. Ask specific questions for feedback. Use testimonials only with permission. Reduce the scope, not your rate.
Offer monthly packages. And report your results honestly. Twelve pitches and no clients yet is still a real start.
